flows.title: The email you have been avoiding for three days
flows.job: A difficult message you know you owe someone
flows.who: anyone who owes a difficult message to a client
flows.situation: A client emailed on Monday and you have read it four times without answering. The tab is still open on your phone at midnight, and every day it sits the reply gets harder to face.
flows.outcome: A four-line email, in your own voice, that you can hit send on the second you finish reading it.
flows.guard: Change one detail to sound like you before it goes.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → ChatGPT → ChatGPT → Gmail → You
flows.prompt: Turn this into a four-line email to a client. Plain words, no apology theatre, keep the ask clear.

steps.do: Write the whole messy version — what happened, what you want, what you are afraid of saying.
Paste it and type: "Turn this into a four-line email to a client. Plain words, no apology theatre, keep the ask clear."
If it came back too soft or too stiff, type: "Rewrite it so I apologise only once and still sound like I mean it."
Paste the draft, put the real name and the real date back in.
Read it out loud once. If it sounds like you, send it.

flows.title: An hour-long meeting into five action items
flows.job: Nobody remembers what was decided
flows.who: the person who has to send the recap after a meeting nobody else owned
flows.situation: An hour of talk, five people on the call, and by the end nobody can say what they each owe. You scribbled fragments while you should have been listening, and now the recap has to come from you.
flows.outcome: A short recap in the room’s thread — decisions made, owners named, open questions flagged — with a subject line that invites correction.
flows.guard: Never record other people without telling them. Notes from your own words are safer.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → Claude → You → Gmail → Google Calendar
flows.prompt: Turn these into decisions made, actions with owners, and anything still undecided.

steps.do: During the meeting, type fragments: names, numbers, decisions. Speed beats grammar.
Paste the fragments: "Turn these into decisions made, actions with owners, and anything still undecided."
Read every action back and check the owner is a real named person and the date is real — not "the team" or "soon".
Send it to the room with the subject line "What we decided — correct me if wrong".
Put every action that has a date into your calendar as an event or task, so it is not just a line in an email you will archive.

flows.title: Read a 40-page document without reading it
flows.job: A contract, a report or a policy you have to understand
flows.who: anyone about to sign or refuse a long document they have not read
flows.situation: A forty-page contract or policy lands in your inbox with a signature due Friday. You do not have two calm hours, but you still need to know exactly what it commits you to before you touch it.
flows.outcome: A one-page note in your own words: the clauses that change what you have to do, their page numbers, and the lines you must still read yourself.
flows.guard: A summary is not advice. For a contract, still read the money and the dates yourself.
flows.arrow: Claude → ChatGPT → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: List the clauses that change what I have to do, with page numbers.

steps.do: Attach or paste the document, then ask: "List the clauses that change what I have to do, with page numbers."
Ask the same question of a second model. Where they disagree is where you must actually read.
Open the pages they both flagged and read the payment, the dates and the exit clause with your own eyes. No summary signs a contract for you.
Paste both answers into a doc and mark only the lines you now understand well enough to sign or refuse.

flows.title: Learn a new subject in one evening, with sources
flows.job: You keep hearing a term and nodding along
flows.who: a student or career-changer meeting a term they keep nodding along to
flows.situation: Everyone keeps saying the word and you smile so nobody notices you do not know it. It is your evening now, and you would rather understand it once, with real sources you can trust, than fake it again on Monday.
flows.outcome: Five lines you can still recall tomorrow morning, and the two or three sources each one came from.
flows.guard: Ask for links, then open one. A model that cites nothing is guessing.
flows.arrow: Perplexity → NotebookLM → ChatGPT → You → Google Keep
flows.prompt: Test me with five questions, one at a time, and tell me where I am wrong.

steps.do: Type the question a beginner would ask, and read the cited sources it returns.
Paste or upload the two sources you trust most and ask it for the differences between them.
Say: "Test me with five questions, one at a time, and tell me where I am wrong."
Score yourself before you read its answers. The ones you flubbed are the ones to re-open — not the ones you already knew.
Write five lines you can still remember tomorrow. Those are the ones you learned.

flows.title: What is in the fridge, turned into tonight’s dinner
flows.job: Food waste and the daily "what do I cook" blank
flows.who: anyone standing at an open fridge with no plan for tonight
flows.situation: It is nearly six, you are tired, and the spinach at the back is going brown. There is real food in there that will be rubbish by Thursday unless something cooks it tonight.
flows.outcome: Tonight’s dinner chosen, and the two or three things you are missing already on a short list you can send yourself.
flows.guard: A model cannot see if meat is off. Your nose still decides.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → Gemini → You → Google Keep → WhatsApp
flows.prompt: Three dinners from these, under 30 minutes, one of them no-cook. Tell me what to throw away first.

steps.do: Type what is in the fridge and cupboard, roughly — "2 eggs, spinach nearly dead, paneer".
Ask: "Three dinners from these, under 30 minutes, one of them no-cook. Tell me what to throw away first."
Overrule the model on anything fresh — meat, dairy, the leftovers at the back. If it smells or looks off, bin it whatever it suggests.
Ask it for the two or three things you are actually missing and keep that as the list.
Text the short shopping list to yourself or the household group, so you buy the two missing things on the way home.

flows.title: A stack of bills into one spreadsheet you can read
flows.job: Money going out of a house or a small shop
flows.who: a household or small shop owner with a pile of bills and no totals
flows.situation: A drawer or inbox of invoices and receipts, and month-end asking where it all went. Every number is there on paper, scattered and useless, until it is one table you can actually read.
flows.outcome: A single spreadsheet with each bill as a row — date, vendor, amount, category — and the category totals you were guessing at.
flows.guard: Never paste bank logins or full card numbers. Amount, date and vendor are enough.
flows.arrow: Google Lens → ChatGPT → Google Sheets → Google Sheets → You
flows.prompt: Turn these into a table with Date, Vendor, Amount, Category. Nothing else.

steps.do: Point the camera app (or lens.google.com) at each bill and copy the text it lifts out.
Paste the text: "Turn these into a table with Date, Vendor, Amount, Category. Nothing else."
Paste the table, then use the formula bar to sum the columns you care about.
Sort or filter the rows by Category so you can see where the money really leaks, not just the grand total.
Match three random rows against the paper. That spot-check is the whole safety step.

flows.title: Kill the blank page for anything you have to write
flows.job: Reports, proposals, cover letters, posts
flows.who: anyone facing a blank page they have to hand in
flows.situation: A report, proposal or cover letter is due and the page is still blank because you cannot see where to begin. The words always come easier once there is something wrong on the screen to correct.
flows.outcome: A finished first draft in your own order, in your own opinion, trimmed of filler and ready to send or edit.
flows.guard: Ask for structure first, prose second — otherwise it writes your opinion for you.
flows.arrow: Claude → Phone notes → Claude → Claude → You
flows.prompt: Use only my bullets and my order, and do not add any opinion I did not write.

steps.do: Describe the reader and the goal, and ask for headings only — no paragraphs yet.
Put your own facts and opinions as rough bullets under each heading. This is the part only you can do.
Write using only your bullets, keeping your order — type: "Use only my bullets and my order, and do not add any opinion I did not write."
The first line is usually throat-clearing. Select just that line and type: "Rewrite only the opening so it starts with the most important fact."
Delete the adjectives and any sentence you would not say out loud.

flows.title: Turn a page full of ads into the four paragraphs
flows.job: Articles that bury the answer under a recipe and a pop-up
flows.who: anyone trying to pull one fact out of an ad-choked page
flows.situation: You clicked in for a single answer and got a cookie banner, a pop-up, and three paragraphs about the writer’s childhood before the point. The fact you need is in there somewhere.
flows.outcome: The four sentences that actually answer your question, and the one source link you can open before you repeat it.
flows.guard: If the page matters, open the original source it quotes. Summaries inherit lies.
flows.arrow: Chrome → Chrome → Gemini → You → Google Keep
flows.prompt: What does this page actually say, and what is filler?

steps.do: Load the article the normal way.
If the page is a wall of ads, click the article body, copy it, and drop the raw text into the chat so you are summarising words, not banners.
Open the side panel and ask: "What does this page actually say, and what is filler?"
If you are going to repeat the fact, open one of its sources first.
Paste the short summary and its source link into a note, so you can cite it tomorrow instead of reopening the page.

flows.title: Photos you took into a post people actually read
flows.job: Shop products, event pictures, travel photos with nothing written
flows.who: a shop, event or travel photographer with photos and no words
flows.situation: You shot the products, the table, the venue — and the photos sit in your camera roll with nothing written, while the post you promised goes out tonight. Naming what is in the frame is easy; making someone care is not.
flows.outcome: One finished caption, in your voice, checked for real names and places, posted beside the photo.
flows.guard: Check names and places. A model will happily invent a neighbourhood.
flows.arrow: ChatGPT → Claude → You → LinkedIn
flows.prompt: Write three captions for this photo: one plain, one warm, one short enough to sit under it.

steps.do: Attach the picture and say who will read the caption and where it goes.
Ask for three tones: plain, warm, and one line that fits under a photo — type: "Write three captions for this photo: one plain, one warm, one short enough to sit under it."
Confirm every name, price and place against what you actually know. A model will invent a neighbourhood to sound specific.
Pick one, fix any detail it got wrong, and post with the photo.

flows.title: Talk for ten minutes, get usable text back
flows.job: Ideas that die because typing them takes too long
flows.who: anyone whose best ideas arrive out loud, not typed
flows.situation: You thought clearly for ten minutes in the car and said nothing you can find now. Typing it out would take an hour, so the recording sat in the app and the idea is already fading.
flows.outcome: A clean readable version of what you said — bullets and one short paragraph — saved beside the raw transcript so nothing you said is lost.
flows.guard: Dictate in a private room — that mic is always the risk, not the model.
flows.arrow: Google Keep → ChatGPT → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: Remove filler, keep my meaning, give me bullet points and one short paragraph.

steps.do: Press the mic and talk unstructured, including the parts you cross out.
Paste the transcript: "Remove filler, keep my meaning, give me bullet points and one short paragraph."
Play back the two or three words the transcript mangled — names, numbers, anything you mumbled — and fix them before this becomes the clean version.
Keep the clean version next to the raw transcript so nothing you said is lost.

flows.title: A five-minute brief before you walk into anyone’s office
flows.job: A meeting with a person you know nothing about
flows.who: anyone about to meet a person they know nothing about
flows.situation: In twenty minutes you are in front of someone whose name you only just read — a new client, a director, a friend of a friend. Walking in cold is the whole dread of the meeting.
flows.outcome: One opening question you can actually remember, grounded in something real about them and their company.
flows.guard: Public facts only. Do not ask a model to describe a private individual.
flows.arrow: Perplexity → Claude → You → Phone notes
flows.prompt: Give me three questions that show I did the reading.

steps.do: Ask for their company’s recent public announcements and the role they hold.
Paste what came back: "Give me three questions that show I did the reading."
Cross off any question that only proves you googled them, and any fact you could not say out loud without wincing. Keep the one you would genuinely ask.
Write the one question you will actually ask. Nobody remembers three.

flows.title: Ask a spreadsheet in English, get the answer
flows.job: A table you cannot analyse because you do not know formulas
flows.who: anyone handed a big spreadsheet they cannot query
flows.situation: A dump of rows lands on you — costs, signups, shipments — and you are meant to answer one question about it, but you do not know a single formula. The file is not the scary part; the blank formula bar is.
flows.outcome: The answer in plain English, and the one formula pasted into a live cell so next month it recalculates without you.
flows.guard: Redact names and IDs before pasting a table. The file leaves your machine at the paste.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → You → Google Sheets
flows.prompt: Which month cost the most, and what formula works this out on its own next month?

steps.do: Delete any column a stranger should not see, then copy the rows.
Paste and ask: "Which month cost the most, and what formula works this out on its own next month?"
Check one cell by hand against a number you already know. A formula that quietly adds the wrong column looks exactly like one that works.
Put the formula in the cell so the answer updates when next month’s number lands.

flows.title: A confusing thing explained on one picture
flows.job: Explaining your process to a new joiner or a client
flows.who: a trainer or team lead explaining a process to someone new
flows.situation: A new joiner, a client or your own boss needs to understand how the thing works — and every time you say it out loud it comes out in a tangle. They need one picture, not another meeting.
flows.outcome: A single diagram — boxes and arrows with the words inside — that one stranger can follow without you standing there.
flows.guard: If it needs a legend to be understood, redraw it with fewer boxes.
flows.arrow: Claude → Canva → You → Canva → Google Docs
flows.prompt: boxes, arrows, and the words inside each box

steps.do: Describe the process and ask for "boxes, arrows, and the words inside each box" — a layout, not an essay.
Use a flowchart or diagram template and drop the words in. Free templates are enough.
Show it to one person who has never done the job. Ask where they got lost.
Where your tester stalled, cut a box or add one, then redraw. The second version is the one that works without you.
Export the diagram and drop it where the next new person will find it — the shared doc or onboarding page, not your desktop.

flows.title: Answer every comment on your post without three hours
flows.job: You posted, people replied, and now the replies pile up
flows.who: a social owner whose post took off and the replies are piling up
flows.situation: You posted, it landed, and now forty comments need a real answer. Ignoring them is how a good post dies; answering each by hand is your whole afternoon gone.
flows.outcome: Every comment answered in your own voice, plus one human line you added yourself at the end of the thread.
flows.guard: Never let a model answer a complaint about money or a legal threat. Those are yours.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → ChatGPT → You → LinkedIn
flows.prompt: Answer each comment in this voice, one or two lines, and leave any that needs a real person for me.

steps.do: Paste the comments that need an answer, one per line.
Paste one of your old replies as an example, then ask for short answers in that voice — type: "Answer each comment in this voice, one or two lines, and leave any that needs a real person for me."
Take by hand any comment about money, a refund or a complaint — never let a draft answer those — and read each reply once before it posts.
Post the replies, then add one human sentence to the thread yourself.

flows.title: A model on your own laptop for things you will not upload
flows.job: Therapy notes, family matters, a client list you must not leak
flows.who: anyone with notes too private to paste into a chatbot
flows.situation: Therapy notes, a family matter, a client list you are not allowed to leak — yet the only model that helps is the one you cannot trust with them. You want something that never touches the internet.
flows.outcome: A small model answering on your own laptop with no network, and a clear line drawn between what goes there and what goes online.
flows.guard: Any laptop from the last five years runs a small model. Do not buy hardware to start.
flows.arrow: Your own laptop → Your own laptop → Your own laptop → HuggingChat → You
flows.prompt: Summarise these meeting notes into three action points.

steps.do: Download Ollama from ollama.com — one installer, no account.
Open the terminal that came with the install and run: ollama run llama3.2:3b.
With the Wi-Fi off, type the thing you would never upload, such as: "Summarise these meeting notes into three action points."
Ask the same private question on HuggingChat and on the local model, then notice which one you would trust.
Decide now which kind of note only ever goes to the local one.

flows.title: A goal turned into the next two weeks only
flows.job: A resolution you wrote in January and forgot by February
flows.who: anyone with a goal they wrote down and quietly dropped
flows.situation: You wrote the goal down with real intention and it has not moved since. A twelve-month plan feels honest in January and impossible by February, so you never start at all.
flows.outcome: A dated fourteen-day plan with at most three actions a day, already sitting as events in your calendar.
flows.guard: If the plan has more than three actions a day, it is a wish. Delete half.
flows.arrow: ChatGPT → Google Calendar → You → Gemini → Google Calendar
flows.prompt: Here is what I actually did — which two things should I stop trying?

steps.do: State the goal and your real weekly hours, then ask for a 14-day plan, three actions a day maximum.
Put the actions in as events. A plan with no slot in it is a wish.
Sweep the two weeks and delete any action you already know you will skip. A plan you keep half of beats a plan you abandon whole.
On day seven ask: "Here is what I actually did — which two things should I stop trying?"
Put the day-seven review in the calendar now, as its own event, or you will never run it.

flows.title: A written script into a short explainer clip
flows.job: Explaining one thing about your product or your work
flows.who: a founder or creator explaining one thing about their product
flows.situation: You need one short video to explain your product, and hiring someone for it is not happening this month. You can write, you can talk — you just cannot edit video from nothing.
flows.outcome: A finished short clip with burned-in captions, exported to your phone or laptop, ready to post.
flows.guard: Free exports carry a watermark or a length cap until you outgrow them — that is fine for a first one.
flows.arrow: Claude → Phone notes → Canva → CapCut → You
flows.prompt: Write a 60-second explainer script, each line with the shot beside it, plain words, no hype.

steps.do: Describe the thing and ask for a 60-second script with the visual noted beside each line — type: "Write a 60-second explainer script, each line with the shot beside it, plain words, no hype."
Read the script out loud once. Anywhere you stumble, shorten the line now, before it costs you a whole take.
Turn the visual column into slides or stock clips — the free assets are enough for a first video.
Import, let it auto-caption, and cut anything longer than four seconds without a change on screen.
Play it with the sound off. If you cannot follow it on captions alone, the message is not in the pictures yet.

flows.title: A tiny script for the chore you do every Friday
flows.job: Renaming files, splitting a list, moving rows between sheets
flows.who: anyone who does the same fiddly computer chore every week
flows.situation: Every Friday you rename the same hundred files, or move the same rows from one sheet to another, by hand. You know a script would do it in seconds, but you do not write code.
flows.outcome: A saved script with a name you will recognise next Friday, proven to work on a copy of your files.
flows.guard: Run it on a copy of your files, never the originals. That is the entire risk.
flows.arrow: ChatGPT → ChatGPT → Your own laptop → ChatGPT → You
flows.prompt: Will this ever overwrite or delete my original files? If so, change it so it only works on a copy.

steps.do: Say what the folder looks like and what it should look like after, and ask for a script plus how to run it.
Before running it, type: "Will this ever overwrite or delete my original files? If so, change it so it only works on a copy."
Make a copy of the folder, then run the script on the copy only.
When it errors, paste the whole error back and ask what to change. Never accept "try again".
Save the working script with a name you will recognise next Friday.

flows.title: Practise the interview you are about to sit
flows.job: A role you want and no one to rehearse with
flows.who: a job seeker about to sit an interview alone
flows.situation: The interview is on Thursday and there is nobody around to practise with. You can feel yourself rambling already, and the silence after each question is exactly where you will lose it.
flows.outcome: Three rehearsed stories with real numbers behind them, and a short list of the weak answers you still have to fix.
flows.guard: A model over-praises. Ask for the harsh version explicitly.
flows.arrow: Perplexity → Claude → Claude → Google Keep → You
flows.prompt: Be harsher. Tell me which answers are weak, where I rambled, and what they really worry you did not cover.

steps.do: Read the job post and the company’s last six months of news, and write down the three things they keep repeating.
Paste those three and ask it to interview you, one question at a time, and grade each answer out of ten.
When it is too kind, type: "Be harsher. Tell me which answers are weak, where I rambled, and what they really worry you did not cover."
Keep three real examples from your work, with the number that proves each one.
Say your lowest-scored answer out loud once more. If it still rambles, cut it to three sentences before Thursday.

flows.title: A letter in another language, explained to your family
flows.job: Official post, a school note, a form you must fill
flows.who: anyone translating official post for a parent or relative
flows.situation: An official letter arrived in a language your mother does not read, and she has been holding it, worried, all week. You need to explain it in her words and answer it — not just get a literal translation.
flows.outcome: The letter understood in your own language, a polite reply drafted in theirs, and the real deadline and reference checked against the paper.
flows.guard: For anything legal, get the official translation too. This is for understanding, not for filing.
flows.arrow: ChatGPT → ChatGPT → Gemini → You
flows.prompt: Now explain what this means to me in five plain sentences — who wants what, by when, and what happens if we ignore it.

steps.do: Upload the picture and ask what it says in your own language, plus the deadline inside it.
Type: "Now explain what this means to me in five plain sentences — who wants what, by when, and what happens if we ignore it."
Draft the response, then ask it to rewrite politely in the official language.
Check the date and the reference number against the paper before anything is sent.

flows.title: Four supplier quotes in four formats into one table you can defend
flows.job: The same part priced four different ways by four different people
flows.who: buyers holding a stack of quote PDFs and one frightened spreadsheet
flows.situation: Everyone sends it their own way. One quotes per thousand with freight inside it, one quotes ex-works with a four-week lead, one sends a number and nothing else. You cannot choose until they sit side by side, and re-typing them takes the morning.
flows.outcome: One row per quote in the same columns, the maths shown underneath, and the two lines you send your manager saying which one you would take and what it costs you in lead time.
flows.guard: Every price, currency and date comes off the real quote, never from the model or from memory. Strip supplier and contact names before you paste if that pricing is confidential to them. Unit, currency, Incoterm and minimum order get read back with your own eyes.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → Chrome → ChatGPT → Claude → You
flows.prompt: Rewrite this as one table normalised to delivered cost per single unit inside 30 days. Show the maths you used for each row. List the terms that are missing and do not guess at them.

steps.do: Make a row per supplier with headers only: unit price, currency, minimum order, lead time, freight, valid until. Leave every cell empty — filling them is the next step.
Open each quote and copy its terms into your row exactly as written, including the odd price breaks. Take the supplier names out while you are in there.

Paste the rows and type: "Rewrite this as one table normalised to delivered cost per single unit inside 30 days. Show the maths you used for each row. List the terms that are missing and do not guess at them."
Paste its table with your real prices beside it and ask: "Two sentences for my manager: which quote to take, what I am trading away to get it, and the one question to put to the runner-up."
Cover the model’s answer and read each price, currency and lead time out of the original quote one more time. One slipped decimal turns the whole table into a rumour.

flows.title: Twenty rows of late receipts into the two suppliers to chase
flows.job: The overdue report everybody complains about and nobody acts on
flows.who: planners who chase whoever emailed last instead of whoever is worst
flows.situation: You can export every late receipt for the quarter, and it is a wall. It always feels like everything is late, so the crew spends the day firefighting whoever shouted loudest this morning. Thirty rows in a paste box ends that argument.
flows.outcome: A ranked shortlist of the suppliers actually costing you days, the pattern behind each one, and the two emails you send before standup.
flows.guard: Paste twenty or thirty rows, not the whole quarter, and strip supplier names if that data is not yours to upload. The grouping is a rough read: check the dates and the count in the sheet yourself before you name anyone to your boss.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Claude → You
flows.prompt: Group these by supplier. For each one give me total days lost, whether this is a one-off or the same thing every month, and one sentence saying what the pattern points at. No advice yet.

steps.do: Open the overdue export and copy only the columns anyone ever asks about: item, original promised date, latest promised date, days late, plant.
Delete the rows you have already closed and the one-day slips nobody is late because of. What is left should be the receipts that actually hurt.

Paste the remaining rows and type: "Group these by supplier. For each one give me total days lost, whether this is a one-off or the same thing every month, and one sentence saying what the pattern points at. No advice yet."
Paste your two worst suppliers back in: "Write one short email to each. State the item, the date I need it on site, and ask for a confirmed ship date. No apologies and no threats."
Match every item, order number and date in those emails against the live report, and send only the lines that still say open.

flows.title: A part on allocation into three substitutes and one good question
flows.job: The component your supplier just said is twelve weeks out
flows.who: planners told a part is end-of-life or allocated, with a build on Thursday
flows.situation: The notification lands and you have no idea what else exists. Engineering are the only people who know the spec and they are in a review until three, so you spend the morning opening datasheets you cannot read properly and pretending to.
flows.outcome: Three candidate substitutes in one table with the specs that genuinely differ, and one three-line question to engineering that gets answered between meetings.
flows.guard: A model matching numbers on a datasheet is not an approval. Anything touching a qualified part, a safety-critical assembly or a customer drawing goes to engineering, and their sign-off is what you record — not this shortlist.
flows.arrow: Chrome → Perplexity → Claude → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: Which other manufacturers make something in this footprint and rating? Give me part numbers and a link to each datasheet, and say where you are unsure.

steps.do: Find the original datasheet and copy out the four numbers a substitute has to match: body size, rating, tolerance, temperature range.
Type the part number and ask: "Which other manufacturers make something in this footprint and rating? Give me part numbers and a link to each datasheet, and say where you are unsure."
Paste your four numbers and the text of each candidate: "Put these in one table and list only the specs that do not match. Say plainly which differences would need a test before we could use it."
Paste the table at the top of a doc and write one question under it: which of these differences we can live with, and what it would take to prove it. Keep it under three lines.
Open each datasheet yourself and confirm the part number and the ratings before you send anything. A model will invent a plausible component nobody makes.

flows.title: A receiving backlog into the four trucks to work first
flows.job: Nine inbound loads and two people on the dock
flows.who: shift leads and inventory clerks facing a queue of inbound
flows.situation: Everything landed at the same time again. Half of it can sweat in the yard; half of it is the pick face that will be empty by two o’clock and stop the pickers. The manifest does not tell you which is which, so the crew starts at the front of the queue and you find out at four.
flows.outcome: A numbered order of work for the dock — which door, which load, what can wait — written where everyone can read it, with room for what changes by lunch.
flows.guard: Quantities and locations come off the real manifest; the model only helps you rank, and it will invent a truck that never departed. Anything with a temperature, safety or delivery deadline you decide yourself.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Gemini → Google Keep → You
flows.prompt: Order these by what will cost me the most in the next six hours. Put the reason in brackets after each line and keep it to a numbered list.

steps.do: Copy the inbound list into a sheet with three columns: what is on the load, where it is going, and whether the pick face for that item is already low.
Paste the rows and type: "Order these by what will cost me the most in the next six hours. Put the reason in brackets after each line and keep it to a numbered list."
Paste that list back: "Turn each line into something a driver can read from four metres away. Ten words or fewer, no jargon, no exclamation marks."
Write the numbered list into a note and put it on the desk screen or the whiteboard, with one blank line at the bottom for whatever changes during the shift.
Stand at the doors for five minutes and check what is physically there against the list. Anything you cannot find moves to the bottom, no matter how urgent the sheet says it is.

flows.title: Forty cycle-count variances into the three worth digging
flows.job: The count never matches the system and nobody knows why
flows.who: inventory clerks and store leads writing off the same numbers weekly
flows.situation: The count sheet comes back with forty differences and you are told to clear them. Most are two units in a bin nobody touches. Three of them are the same aisle, the same shift and the same size class — and that is the actual problem, buried under the noise.
flows.outcome: The patterns behind the variances, the bins you recount today, and one paragraph for the weekly meeting that explains the number instead of apologising for it.
flows.guard: Do not let a model adjust, write off or explain a quantity. Every variance you act on gets recounted on the floor first, and if your inventory file is confidential, strip supplier and customer names before pasting.
flows.arrow: Excel → ChatGPT → Google Sheets → Claude → You
flows.prompt: Group these variances and tell me the three patterns that explain the most units lost. Do not suggest fixes. Say what I would need to check to be sure of each one.

steps.do: Open the count export and keep only location, item, system quantity, counted quantity, shift. Delete everything else so the paste stays small.
Paste the rows and type: "Group these variances and tell me the three patterns that explain the most units lost. Do not suggest fixes. Say what I would need to check to be sure of each one."
Back in the sheet, filter by aisle and by shift and count the variances yourself. If a pattern the model named does not survive that filter, drop it and stop mentioning it.
Paste the two patterns you confirmed: "Write one paragraph for my weekly meeting. Give the number, the likely reason, what I am doing this week, and what I am not claiming yet."
Go and recount two bins from each pattern before you send a word of it. Two honest recounts tell you more than any analysis on a screen.

flows.title: A thirty-stop manifest into a morning run you can actually drive
flows.job: Sequencing the vans by hand every single morning
flows.who: dispatchers and drivers building the daily run list
flows.situation: The stops arrive in the order the orders came in. You spend twenty minutes shuffling them on a printout, and half the day is still backtracking because a delivery window was hiding in a notes column nobody reads.
flows.outcome: A numbered stop list grouped by area with the timed ones pinned to the front, the two or three you are rescheduling to tomorrow, and the whole thing already in the driver’s phone.
flows.guard: The model does not know about the low bridge, the one-way, the market day or the gate that closes at eleven. Cut addresses down to area or postcode before pasting if the customer data is not yours to upload, then drive the order yourself.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Google Sheets → Gemini → WhatsApp → You
flows.prompt: Group these into runs that stay inside one area, order them with the timed windows first, and list any stop that looks like it belongs in a different group.

steps.do: Copy the manifest into three columns only: area or postcode, required window, and what is on the stop. Take the street names and customer names out.
Paste the rows and type: "Group these into runs that stay inside one area, order them with the timed windows first, and list any stop that looks like it belongs in a different group."
Reorder the list yourself where it is wrong about your patch. Write the reason next to anything you moved, so you can explain it at four o’clock.
Paste the finished order: "Turn this into one short line per stop for a driver: stop number, area, time window, what to watch for. No explanations."
Send the list into the driver group as text, not a screenshot, so it is still searchable three stops down the road.
Count the stops and read the last time window against the clock before anybody leaves the yard.

flows.title: This morning’s delay list into an honest message per customer
flows.job: Twelve shipments late and twelve people who have not been told
flows.who: dispatchers and the customer-facing half of a delivery team
flows.situation: The carrier sends one line about disruption on three lanes at 06:50. You know which of your customers are on those lanes and none of them know yet. Writing twelve careful messages takes an hour you do not have, so you do three and hope for the best.
flows.outcome: A short, honest message per affected shipment in your drafts, each with the real reference and the next update time, plus a reminder set for when you promised to come back.
flows.guard: Use the dates the carrier gave you, never one the model thinks is nicer, and promise no compensation, no replacement and no guaranteed delivery time. Strip customer names before pasting if their account is confidential, then put them back by hand.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → Claude → Gmail → ChatGPT → Google Calendar → You
flows.prompt: Write one message per shipment. Say what happened, the date I have from the carrier, and when I will next update. No apology paragraphs and no promises I did not give you.

steps.do: List the late shipments with the lane, the reference number and a first name only. Nothing else about the account leaves your machine.
Paste them and type: "Write one message per shipment. Say what happened, the date I have from the carrier, and when I will next update. No apology paragraphs and no promises I did not give you."
Put each message into its own draft with the reference in the subject line, then paste the real tracking number and full name back in from the system.
For the accounts already late twice: "Rewrite this one so it owns the problem, gives a firm next update time, and does not blame the carrier in front of my customer."
Put a fifteen-minute reminder in for tomorrow at the update time you just promised, so the second message is not another surprise.
Read each draft against the tracking screen before you press send. A wrong reference number is a second angry call you did not need.

flows.title: A line that stopped twice into a log entry that means something
flows.job: The maintenance log that is blank because nobody has time to write it
flows.who: operators, technicians and production leads with a paper log
flows.situation: The press stopped for eleven minutes, then again after the break. The tech fixed it, the operator went back to running, and by the end of shift nobody can say what it actually was. Next month it happens again and three people start from nothing.
flows.outcome: Two log lines in the same wording every time — fault, duration, what was done, what to watch — plus the one question you are leaving for the next shift.
flows.guard: Times, machine numbers and what was done come from you or the panel, never from the summary. Anything safety-related goes through your incident process, and that is a human call, not a tidy piece of writing.
flows.arrow: Google Keep → Claude → ChatGPT → Excel → You
flows.prompt: Turn this into four short fields: fault, duration, action taken, watch next shift. Fifteen words each and no detail I did not give you.

steps.do: Press the mic the moment the machine is running again and say it out loud: what stopped, roughly how long, what you touched, what you are still not sure about. Messy is fine.
Paste or retype the note and ask: "Turn this into four short fields: fault, duration, action taken, watch next shift. Fifteen words each and no detail I did not give you."
Paste both events and type: "Rewrite these so they follow exactly the same wording pattern, so a year of these logs can be read as one list."
Add the rows to your downtime sheet with the real machine number, the real start time and the real duration off the clock or the panel.
Read the entry back against what you actually did and put anything the summary smoothed over. A log is evidence, not prose.

flows.title: The question you answer four times a shift into one posted card
flows.job: Tribal knowledge that lives in one person’s head
flows.who: production leads whose team keeps walking over to ask the same thing
flows.situation: Every shift someone asks how that tool is set up, or who to call when the label printer jams. You answer it perfectly from memory, and it takes four minutes each time. Tomorrow someone asks again, and you are on leave.
flows.outcome: A one-page card taped at the machine: the three most-asked questions, the answer in six short steps, and who to get when the card is wrong.
flows.guard: Write the machine settings yourself, off the actual machine and the spec sheet. A model will happily invent a plausible temperature or torque. Numbers get checked before anything is printed and posted.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → Google Sheets → Claude → Canva → You
flows.prompt: Turn this into six numbered steps a person could follow with gloves on. Short sentences. Flag every step where a number depends on the machine.

steps.do: For two shifts, write down every question that walks to your desk, one line each, in the exact words the person used.
Sort the list and keep the three that came up most often. The other fifteen are not the problem, and nobody reads a page with eighteen answers on it.
Paste one question with your own rough answer: "Turn this into six numbered steps a person could follow with gloves on. Short sentences. Flag every step where a number depends on the machine."
Drop the three answers into a plain A4 template — big type, one question per block, and a blank line at the bottom that says ask if this is not what you see. Free templates are enough.
Hand it to someone who has never done that job and stand back while they read it. Fix the line they stall on, then print it and put it on the machine.

flows.title: A forty-line availability report into the transfers worth writing
flows.job: Dead stock in one store, a waiting list in another
flows.who: shop managers, territory reps and franchise owners moving stock between sites
flows.situation: The weekly report says thirty-eight lines are out of stock somewhere. Half need a head office order; half are sitting eleven miles away in another store’s back room where nobody will look. The report is built to be printed, so you cannot see the pairings.
flows.outcome: A transfer list of eight to ten lines with from, to and quantity, and one short message to each store saying what is leaving and what is arriving.
flows.guard: Move only quantities the system actually shows on hand, and check both sides before the paperwork goes out. Store numbers beat store names in the paste — cut anything confidential about owners or customers.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Claude → WhatsApp → You
flows.prompt: Find the lines where one site has too much and another has none. Give me the transfer, the quantity, and say plainly where you cannot tell because a number is missing.

steps.do: Copy two lists out of the report for every site: lines showing zero on hand, and lines showing more than three weeks of cover. Keep the store number, drop the name.
Paste both lists and type: "Find the lines where one site has too much and another has none. Give me the transfer, the quantity, and say plainly where you cannot tell because a number is missing."
Paste the matches back: "Rank these by what a customer asks for at the counter this week, not by value. Ten lines maximum and one reason each."
Send each site a short message: what is leaving, what is arriving, when. Text, not a screenshot, so it is still findable on Sunday.
Open the stock screen for every line you are about to move and confirm the quantity on hand. A transfer written against yesterday’s number becomes a second stock-out.

flows.title: Next week’s roster into the four hours you have not covered
flows.job: Six staff, eleven constraints, and a shop open seven days
flows.who: shop managers and franchise owners building the weekly rota
flows.situation: You build the rota in your head, post it, and by Tuesday it collapses because someone is on a course and two people only do afternoons. The holes are always in the corner you stopped looking at after the second pass.
flows.outcome: A rota draft with every uncovered hour listed on its own line, two swap requests you can actually send, and a clean version you can post on Thursday.
flows.guard: A model does not know your rest-break rules, young-worker limits or anything your own policy requires — check the finished rota against that policy yourself before it goes on the board. First names and availability only in the paste.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Copilot → Excel → You
flows.prompt: Fill the coverage minimums first. Then list every hour still uncovered, by day, and do not invent shifts to make the list look tidy.

steps.do: Write your trading hours per day and the minimum people you need at open, at peak and at close. Do this before you look at who is free.
Paste the hours you need and everyone’s availability and type: "Fill the coverage minimums first. Then list every hour still uncovered, by day, and do not invent shifts to make the list look tidy."
Paste the uncovered hours and the three people who are nearly free: "Give me the two swaps that cover the most hours with the least disruption, and a polite two-line message to ask for each."
Type the pattern back into your own rota sheet, your formatting and your names. Keep the model’s text out of the document that goes on the wall.
Check rest days, shift maxima and anything your policy requires with your eyes. This rota is your call, and the draft is only a draft.

flows.title: A two-star review streak into the one listing change worth making
flows.job: Thirty reviews that all say something and none say what
flows.who: marketplace sellers and storefront operators watching a rating slide
flows.situation: The score dropped from four and a half to under four in six weeks and there are twenty-two new reviews. You read four, they each say something different, so you change nothing. Somewhere in that pile is one sentence a buyer needed to read before ordering.
flows.outcome: The two complaints that genuinely repeat, the exact line to add to your listing, and one honest question for your supplier about the rest.
flows.guard: Paste review text with buyer names, order numbers and dates stripped out. Change no size, material or claim the product does not actually meet, and never send a review reply you have not read yourself.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Claude → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: Group these complaints by what a buyer could have avoided by reading the listing. Count each group. Ignore anything that is just someone being rude.

steps.do: Copy the last thirty reviews into a sheet: the text, the star count, and which variation they bought. Delete names, order numbers and dates before you go further.
Paste them and type: "Group these complaints by what a buyer could have avoided by reading the listing. Count each group. Ignore anything that is just someone being rude."

Paste the biggest group and your current bullet points: "Write the one sentence that belongs on the listing so this surprises nobody. Plain, honest, no marketing words, and nothing I did not give you."
Under it, write the question for your maker or supplier about the second group: what fails, how often, what you want changed. Five lines, no drama.
Read the new line while holding the actual item. If you cannot point at it on the product, delete it. Then make the change.

flows.title: A bare SKU dump into titles a search can actually find
flows.job: Two hundred listings named by code and nothing else
flows.who: catalogue operators and marketplace sellers with a spreadsheet of parts
flows.situation: Your catalogue is a wall of codes. The customer searches for the plain words for the thing and you simply do not exist. Every attribute you would need is already in the sheet — it has just never been turned into the words a person types.
flows.outcome: Ten rewritten titles and bullets built only from your own attributes, plus the one-page rule your colleague copies for the other hundred and ninety.
flows.guard: Use only the specs in your own sheet. No size, material, standard or approval the model adds, and no claims about fitness for anything. Search words come from real customer messages and the platform’s own search bar.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → Perplexity → ChatGPT → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: What words do buyers actually search for this? List the common phrasings, the synonyms and the usual mistakes, with sources I can click.

steps.do: Split the code into columns: item type, material, size, finish, pack quantity. If a column is empty for most rows, delete it rather than guessing at it.
Describe the item plainly and ask: "What words do buyers actually search for this? List the common phrasings, the synonyms and the usual mistakes, with sources I can click."
Paste ten cleaned rows and type: "Write one title and three bullets per row using only the attributes I gave you. Put the searched word near the front. Add no spec that is not in the row."
Paste the best two and the weakest one into a doc with one sentence each saying why. That page is what the next hundred and ninety get copied from.
Line each title up against the row it came from: size, thread, material, pack count. Change five in the real catalogue and look at them live before you touch the rest.

flows.title: A worried payslip question answered the same hour
flows.job: An employee is sure the payroll is wrong
flows.who: HR generalists and office managers who answer payroll questions they did not calculate
flows.situation: A message lands at 4:40pm: "my pay is wrong again, can someone check". They have a mortgage and a bad month behind them, and you have the payslip, the contract and no idea yet whether they are right. Leaving it until tomorrow makes it a worse conversation.
flows.outcome: A reply that names the exact lines you checked, says which one you are still confirming and gives a real date — plus the short note that goes to payroll.
flows.guard: Strip the payslip to hours, rate, deduction names and amounts before it goes anywhere — no tax ID, no bank account, no date of birth, no employee name in the chat box. And do not let a model tell someone they are wrong: until payroll confirms it, this is a query, not an error.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → Claude → ChatGPT → Gmail → Google Calendar → You
flows.prompt: List every way these numbers could disagree. Say which line I must confirm with payroll and which one I can answer from this.

steps.do: Type the two lines as the employee put them, then the three payslip lines involved — hours, rate, deduction name and amount. No name, no ID.
Paste those lines and ask: "List every way these numbers could disagree. Say which line I must confirm with payroll and which one I can answer from this."

Give it the mismatch list and type: "Write two replies to someone who thinks they are underpaid: one under 60 words, one that shows the arithmetic. Plain words, no apology theatre, and do not admit or deny an error."
Send the shorter one, copy payroll so the confirmation is not only your promise, and paste the amount you checked into the thread so nobody re-derives it.
Put the follow-up you committed to in as a morning event, before you close the laptop. An unpromised date is the thing they remember.
Read the reply as the person who typed at 4:40pm. Does it say who is doing what, by when, and what happens if they are right? If not, add one line.

flows.title: Four interviews for one role, scored the same way
flows.job: A panel where everyone asks their own questions
flows.who: hiring managers running three interviewers and no shared bar
flows.situation: Four candidates this week, three interviewers, and each one has their own favourite list of questions and their own private idea of what good sounds like. By Friday the decision will come down to who talked most enthusiastically in the corridor, and you will not be able to explain it to the two you reject.
flows.outcome: One page: four month-one tasks, the question for each, what a strong answer contains, and a 1-4 grid every interviewer fills in before they speak to each other.
flows.guard: The model does not know your team, so it will hand you generic questions unless you give it the actual tasks. Keep the notes factual rather than adjectival — they can be read back later — and treat the scorecard as discipline, not as a defence.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → ChatGPT → Claude → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: For each task, one interview question that would show whether they have done it, what a strong answer contains, and what a weak one sounds like.

steps.do: Type four things this person has to be able to do in their first month, as tasks: "rebuild the returns sheet without asking", not "detail-oriented".
Paste the four tasks and type: "For each task, one interview question that would show whether they have done it, what a strong answer contains, and what a weak one sounds like."
Paste the questions back and type: "Give each question a 1-4 scale with one plain sentence for what each level means, so three people cannot score the same answer differently."
One row per question: the question, what strong looks like, the 1-4 boxes, a column per interviewer and one line at the end for the evidence they saw.
Read each question aloud and answer it from your own memory of the job. If you cannot tell a 2 from a 3, the question is too vague — replace it now, not on Wednesday.

flows.title: Six exit interviews into the four things to fix
flows.job: Keeping the reasons people actually leave
flows.who: HR and team leads losing the same kind of person on repeat
flows.situation: Four people left in one quarter. You have a document per exit — half of it is your own shorthand, two are the manager’s version of the same conversation, and one is a polite paragraph from someone who did not want trouble. None of it is connected to the two who stayed and are quietly looking.
flows.outcome: One page with the four repeated causes, the exact quote sitting under each, and two changes you can name at the next all-hands — kept beside the raw notes so nobody calls it editorial.
flows.guard: In a team of nine, "the shift lead" is a name — so strip every person, department and identifying detail before pasting, and keep the quotes verbatim rather than let a model rewrite them. It will flatten real nuance into tidy corporate clichés, and a tidy cliché is useless in a meeting.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → Claude → ChatGPT → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: Group these into causes, most repeated first. Under each, quote the exact words that belong there and say how many people said something close.

steps.do: Paste all the exit notes one after another, labelled A to F, and delete any line that names a person, a manager or a team small enough to identify.
Paste the whole doc and type: "Group these into causes, most repeated first. Under each, quote the exact words that belong there and say how many people said something close."

steps.chip: is it the job or them
steps.do: Paste the same notes into a second model and ask: "What in here is about one manager rather than about the job? Say which cause collapses if you remove that one person."
For the top two causes, open your own notes and find the quoted line. One quote means a feeling, not a pattern — and where the two models disagree is the paragraph you have to read again yourself.
Under the list, write the two changes you can actually make, who you will say them to, and the sentence you will use. Save it beside the raw notes.

flows.title: The month-end number that jumped, explained in one line
flows.job: Someone asks why this month costs four thousand more
flows.who: bookkeepers, controllers and owners who are also the finance department
flows.situation: The month closed and one line is way off — above last month, above the plan, and you have forty minutes before the call where somebody asks. Two of the movers are genuine, one looks like a duplicate charge, and one is a subscription nobody remembers approving.
flows.outcome: A short table: each suspicious line, the amount, the two boring explanations, and the one question to ask a supplier or a colleague before you write anything off.
flows.guard: Redact account numbers, supplier bank details and anything identifying a customer before you paste — date, counterparty, category and amount are enough. A model is excellent at inventing a plausible reason, so every reason it offers is a question to ask, not an answer to record. Do not post a journal on its guess.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Google Sheets → Claude → You
flows.prompt: Here are two months. List the lines that moved most, biggest first, and for each give the two boring explanations and the one thing I should check.

steps.do: Put the two months side by side, then delete every column a stranger should not see. Keep date, counterparty, category and amount.
Copy the rows in and type: "Here are two months. List the lines that moved most, biggest first, and for each give the two boring explanations and the one thing I should check."
Add a column called checked and mark the lines only you can see — approvals, who ordered it, whether the period is right. That column is the real work.
Paste your table and ask: "Write the two-line answer I give the owner: the number that moved most, what is already explained, and what I am confirming by Friday."
Open the two biggest movers in the actual ledger and compare the figures. If they are not there, your paste was wrong and every reason above them is fiction.

flows.title: An unpaid list turned into a chase that actually gets paid
flows.job: Chasing twelve customers without sounding rude or desperate
flows.who: freelancers, bookkeepers and small-business owners sending the same awkward email twelve times
flows.situation: The ageing list is twelve names and thirty-days-past is the fat one. You have chased three of them verbally and nothing moved. You need to write to all of them today, except each is a person you see again, and the tone you used last time plainly did not work.
flows.outcome: Three short emails — a nudge, a firm one with a due date, and a last one before work pauses — plus every invoice filed under which one it gets and on what day.
flows.guard: Never let a model invent an invoice number, an amount or a date: those come from your sheet, and one wrong figure turns a reminder into a dispute. Leave out interest, late fees and legal language unless your terms already say it and your accountant agrees — a threatened penalty that is not in the contract costs you the customer and the argument.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → ChatGPT → Google Docs → Claude → Gmail → You
flows.prompt: Sort these into three groups by days late and size: gentle nudge, firm with a date, and last one before we pause work. Say which invoices land where and why.

steps.do: Bring the overdue list into a sheet with invoice number, issue date, days late and amount. Delete your internal notes and staff names.
Paste the rows and type: "Sort these into three groups by days late and size: gentle nudge, firm with a date, and last one before we pause work. Say which invoices land where and why."
Draft the three emails once each, leaving the invoice number, the amount and the due date as obvious gaps you will fill from the sheet.
Paste the three drafts: "Make these less apologetic without making them colder. Keep each under 90 words and never use the phrase ‘valued customer’ or ‘following up on my previous email’."
Send the first group now, pasting the numbers from the sheet rather than retyping them, and schedule the second group for the same weekday next week.
Read the invoice number and the amount in every email against your own sheet before they leave. That single mistake is the one that makes you look wrong instead of early.

flows.title: The invoice that does not match the order, in five differences
flows.job: Approving a supplier bill against the quote you signed
flows.who: AP clerks, ops managers and anyone whose job is to say yes or no to a bill
flows.situation: An invoice lands as a PDF, the total is higher than the signed quote, and the person who ordered it is on site with no signal. The four of you have minutes before the payment run closes, so somebody is going to guess — and guessing here means a supplier chasing you next month.
flows.outcome: A difference list between the two documents — line, quantity, unit price, dates, reference — each marked same, different, or it could not be read, ready to paste into the mail to the supplier.
flows.guard: Both documents go in as text with bank details and registration numbers stripped. A model reads a 1 as a 7 off a scan and will happily report a difference that is not there, so every mismatch is checked against the PDF before you hold a payment — and nothing here decides the tax treatment, which is your accountant’s call.
flows.arrow: Google Lens → Google Docs → Claude → You → Gmail
flows.prompt: Compare these two documents line by line. Give me a table: item, in the quote, on the invoice, same or different, and anything you could not read clearly.

steps.do: If it came on paper, point the camera app at each page and copy the text it lifts out. For a PDF, open it in Chrome and copy the visible text instead.
Put the quote and the invoice into one document under two headings, then delete the bank lines, account numbers and any sort code before you ask anything.
Type: "Compare these two documents line by line. Give me a table: item, in the quote, on the invoice, same or different, and anything you could not read clearly."
Open the invoice itself and read the three largest differences with your own eyes. Keep only the ones that are real and note which document you believe.
Send the difference table to the supplier, one line per mismatch, ask which document is correct, and copy the person who placed the order.

flows.title: Fifty reviews turned into twelve angles you have not used
flows.job: Writing copy when everything sounds like everything else
flows.who: marketing owners with a pile of reviews and a brief that says make it pop
flows.situation: You have written the same three claims for months — fast, friendly, good value — and the click rate keeps sliding down. Meanwhile your customers have been telling you exactly why they bought, in their own words, in reviews you have never read past the five-star ones.
flows.outcome: Twelve hooks, each one carrying the quote that inspired it and where to use it, so you can prove the claim before you spend anything testing it.
flows.guard: Public reviews only, with names, photos and anything identifying a reviewer removed before pasting, and never turn a customer’s experience into a claim about what your product does. A model will overstate what someone said, so every hook needs its quote sitting beside it: no quote, no hook.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → ChatGPT → Claude → Google Sheets → You
flows.prompt: Group these by the reason someone bought and the thing that nearly stopped them. Two short quotes under each group, nothing else.

steps.do: Paste thirty to fifty recent reviews as plain text, one per line, names gone. Keep the bad ones — that is where the objections live.
Type: "Group these by the reason someone bought and the thing that nearly stopped them. Two short quotes under each group, nothing else."
Paste the groups back and ask: "For each group, three hooks under 12 words that start from that customer’s own words. No exclamation marks and no invented facts."
One row per hook: the hook, the quote it came from, and where it goes — subject line, first three seconds of a clip, ad headline.
Cross out every hook you cannot tie back to a quote on its row. That is usually a third of them, and the rest are worth paying for.

flows.title: Twenty minutes of a real conversation into a week of posts
flows.job: Nothing left to say about your own product
flows.who: founders and solo marketers who only ever talk to themselves online
flows.situation: The calendar is empty again, because everything you can say about your own product you have already said. But yesterday you spent twenty minutes with a customer and you remember three things they said that surprised you — except you did not write any of them down, and by Friday you will only remember the feeling.
flows.outcome: Five posts in your own voice, each built on one thing a real person said, plus the question you still need answered so the next call fixes it.
flows.guard: Ask before you reuse anything from a customer call, then strip the company name, the numbers and the person — and do not upload a recording to a random site to get a transcript when your own phone notes will do. Keep the fumbles in: that is usually where the useful sentence is.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → Google Keep → Claude → ChatGPT → LinkedIn → You
flows.prompt: Pick the five things here only someone who has done this job would say. Under each, one short post in plain English and one question to ask next time.

steps.do: Before you forget, write what you remember in their words: the question that stopped them, the thing they complained about, the two bits you missed.
Press the mic and talk through the same call for ninety seconds instead of typing it, then copy that transcript under your notes. Speech gets the phrases back.
Paste notes and transcript and type: "Pick the five things here only someone who has done this job would say. Under each, one short post in plain English and one question to ask next time."
Paste one old post of yours plus the five drafts: "Rewrite these in the style of my example — same sentence length, no marketing words, and do not add any fact I did not give you."
Post the two strongest this week and put the question from a third one in the first comment, where the people who care will find it.
Read all five against your notes. Any figure, name or detail that is not in the notes came from the model — cut it or go and verify it before posting.

flows.title: The email nobody opens past the first two lines
flows.job: Rewriting the top of an email that is losing readers
flows.who: newsletter owners and marketing leads watching an open rate slide for four sends
flows.situation: You know the number that matters is clicks, and it has fallen four sends running. Your hunch is the opening has gone soft — a greeting, a hope-you-are-well, and the actual news down on line eight where nobody gets. You cannot see it any more, because you wrote it.
flows.outcome: Six ways to start, the one that is most like you, the paragraph from the middle that is now gone, and the email sent to yourself so you see it in a real inbox.
flows.guard: A model will make your opening sound like every other marketing email unless you feed it your own old ones as the only style it may use. Do not let it add a statistic, a customer or a deadline you did not give it — an invented offer is the fastest way to lose a list.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → ChatGPT → Claude → Gmail → You
flows.prompt: Using only my four old openings as the style, write six ways to start this email so the news is in the first line. No greeting, no question opener, 30 words each.

steps.do: Paste this week’s draft, then under a heading the opening two lines from the four emails that performed best. Those four are the style sample.
Type: "Using only my four old openings as the style, write six ways to start this email so the news is in the first line. No greeting, no question opener, 30 words each."
Paste the draft and ask: "Which sentences in the middle could be deleted without losing the point? List each one with the reason it is safe to cut."
Put your chosen opening in, keep one of its phrases and change one word to yours, then send it to yourself and look at it on your phone in a real inbox.
With the preview pane closed, read the top two lines. If the news still is not there, the model did not help and the opening is yours to rewrite by hand.

flows.title: The question you answered nine times, written down once
flows.job: Turning a repeating request into a page customers can find
flows.who: support agents and owners whose knowledge base is one person’s memory
flows.situation: Nine people this fortnight asked some version of the same thing — the return window, why the app logs out, what comes in the box. You answered each one politely and wrote nothing down, so the tenth gets the same typing from you at 4pm on a Friday.
flows.outcome: One plain page: the question in the words customers actually use, the four-line answer, the two edge cases, and the reply you paste next time instead of composing.
flows.guard: Take the wording from real tickets with names, order numbers and emails removed. A model will make your policy sound tidy and certain even when it is neither, so anything about refunds, warranty or delivery timing goes back to what your terms actually say before it is published anywhere.
flows.arrow: Gmail → Claude → ChatGPT → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: Merge these into one page: the question in the words a customer would use, the answer in four lines, and every place my five answers disagree with each other.

steps.do: Search the last two months for the phrase you keep typing, open the five answers you are happiest with and copy them into one doc, names and order numbers stripped out.
Paste the five and type: "Merge these into one page: the question in the words a customer would use, the answer in four lines, and every place my five answers disagree with each other."
Paste the merged page: "Write the three questions a customer asks after reading this, and the two-sentence answer to each, using only what I gave you."
Open your terms and the product itself and confirm every day, cost and limit on the page. The disagreement between your own five replies is the real question — settle it before anyone else has to.
Save as one page with a title a customer would type, put the paste-able answer at the very top, and send the link to whoever owns the help centre.

flows.title: Saying no to a refund without losing the customer
flows.job: A decent person asking for money your policy will not return
flows.who: support agents and owners who decide the awkward money cases themselves
flows.situation: They want their money back and they are being civil about it, which makes it harder. The item is past the window, their complaint about the product is genuinely correct, and the answer is no. You have typed and deleted four versions and you are dreading the reply.
flows.outcome: A reply that says no once and clearly, admits the part they are right about, offers the one thing you are allowed to do, and two lines ready for if they push back.
flows.guard: You decide the outcome — a model is trained to please and will happily promise a refund, a credit or a replacement your terms do not allow. Keep personal details out of the chat box; the order facts and dates are enough. Anything involving a chargeback, a complaint body or a lawyer is yours to answer or escalate, never to automate.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → ChatGPT → Claude → You → Gmail
flows.prompt: Draft a reply that says no to the refund once, plainly, then offers this instead. Admit the fault, do not over-apologise, five sentences maximum.

steps.do: Type the four facts with no name attached: what they bought, the order and return dates, what is actually wrong with the product, and the one thing you are allowed to offer.
Paste the facts and type: "Draft a reply that says no to the refund once, plainly, then offers this instead. Admit the fault, do not over-apologise, five sentences maximum."
Paste the draft: "Give me the two lines to use if they reply that they will dispute the charge, and one closing line that does not repeat the no."
Check it against your actual terms and the dates on the order, then change the greeting and one sentence so it sounds like you. If it reads like a policy document, rewrite the middle.
Send it and add a note to the order record: what you offered, what you declined and why, so the next person does not hand out the refund by accident.

flows.title: Thirty sticky notes into five things people will actually do
flows.job: A retro nobody wants because nothing ever changes
flows.who: scrum masters and team leads whose action list never survives one sprint
flows.situation: The board is full of notes, three of them are the same complaint in different colours, one is about the person who left, and the room has fifteen minutes left. Last sprint you wrote six actions and nobody has mentioned any of them since, which is why half of this board is sarcasm.
flows.outcome: Four causes named in the team’s own words, one action each with a person and a date beside it, and a block you can paste straight into the doc the next retro opens on.
flows.guard: Strip anything that names a colleague before pasting — you are not asking a model to rank your team. Its groupings are guesses, so hold them against the notes, and one action per cause with an owner and a date is the whole difference between a retro and a wall of wishes.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → Claude → ChatGPT → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: Group these into causes, biggest first. Use the sharpest line in the group as its heading, and tell me which notes fit nowhere.

steps.do: Type every note as a single line with no names on it, plus the two things the room said out loud that nobody wrote down.
Paste the lines and type: "Group these into causes, biggest first. Use the sharpest line in the group as its heading, and tell me which notes fit nowhere."
Paste the four causes: "For each, one action we could finish inside one sprint, and the thing we will look at next retro to know whether it worked."
Put the four under last sprint’s actions and mark each one done, still open, or dropped — with the reason. An action list that never gets closed out is why nobody believes the next one.
Say each action aloud to the room and ask who owns it and by when. If nobody answers with a name and a date, delete it and stop pretending it is an action.

flows.title: A slipped date turned into a message a client can act on
flows.job: Telling someone important that the date has moved
flows.who: project managers and freelancers who owe a status mail they keep putting off
flows.situation: The build is two weeks late, three things caused it, and the client meeting is Thursday. You can see the whole mess in your head, but every version you start typing sounds either like an excuse or like a technical report — and the client has been telling their own board your old date for a month.
flows.outcome: A short mail with the new date first, two options with what each costs, one plain sentence on the cause — and three bullets in the same words for Thursday.
flows.guard: Do not let a model choose the date or the trade-off: it will agree to whatever sounds calm, including a delivery day you know is impossible. Give it only facts from your own plan, and name the cause plainly — a vague reason costs more trust than an ugly one.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → ChatGPT → Claude → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: Using only these, write a five-line update to a client: the new date first, one sentence on why, then two options with what each costs. No apology paragraph.

steps.do: Write what moved, the old date and the new one, the two causes you can state without blaming a named person, and what you could cut to buy time back.
Paste the facts and type: "Using only these, write a five-line update to a client: the new date first, one sentence on why, then two options with what each costs. No apology paragraph."
Paste the draft: "What three questions will this cause, and what is the shortest honest answer to each? One of them will be about blame — answer that one carefully."
Put the mail and the three answers on one page, add the two dates you can genuinely commit to, and keep the page open during the meeting.
Read every date against the plan and every name against who is still on the project. Then read it as the client, who has to forward it to someone above them.

flows.title: A twelve-page procedure into the one page people actually follow
flows.job: The SOP that is correct but unread
flows.who: ops managers and team leads who keep re-explaining the same process
flows.situation: The procedure is current, approved, and eleven pages long. Every mistake the team makes sits in a paragraph on page nine. You have started answering it in person instead, which means the document is now decoration.
flows.outcome: One printed page: the five steps in order, the two places it usually goes wrong, and who to tell when it does.
flows.guard: If the procedure is internal, do not paste company names, system names or staff details into a chat box — swap them for placeholders, or run the whole thing on Your own laptop. The short version must still match the original word for word on numbers, form names and thresholds; that check is yours, and a model will smooth a deadline into a suggestion.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → Claude → Google Docs → Gemini → You → You
flows.prompt: Turn this into one page: five numbered steps, each starting with a verb. Then list the two places a new person most often gets this wrong, and the one sentence for who to tell when it breaks. No headings I did not ask for.

steps.do: Copy the whole procedure into a blank doc and strip the styling so it is plain text you can paste anywhere.

Paste the text, then type: "Turn this into one page: five numbered steps, each starting with a verb. Then list the two places a new person most often gets this wrong, and the one sentence for who to tell when it breaks. No headings I did not ask for."
Start a second blank doc, paste the one page in, set the font big enough to read at a laminator distance, and save it as a PDF.
Open a fresh chat, paste only the one page, and ask: "What are the first three things I do, and who signs step four?" If it cannot answer, the page is too clever — cut it again.
Read the one page against the original line by line: each threshold, form name, deadline and sign-off. Fix what drifted before anything gets printed.
Tape the printed page where the work happens and watch one person follow it without asking you anything. The step they still ask about is the step you got wrong.

flows.title: Thirty emails and no decision into one page with a name on it
flows.job: The vendor thread four people will not close
flows.who: ops and procurement people chasing a yes or no that is six weeks late
flows.situation: Fourteen emails, two people on leave, one quote that changed twice. Everyone agrees the thread is a mess. Nobody is going to be the one who says what was actually decided.
