flows.outcome: A four-line decision note sent to the same distribution: what we pick, what it costs, who actioned it, and the date it is closed.
flows.guard: Prices, contract values and supplier names are commercially sensitive — paste the thread to Your own laptop, or blank the amounts and names before you upload anywhere. Nothing here commits money: the decision stays yours, and a model will happily record an option someone rejected as though it were agreed.
flows.arrow: Gmail → Google Docs → Claude → Google Docs → You → Gmail
flows.prompt: List every decision actually agreed, every option still open, and every promise made by a named person with the date it was made. Quote the line it came from. Do not summarise what is not in the text.

steps.do: Open the thread, select all messages, and copy them into one plain-text block — sender, date and body, in order.
Search and replace the supplier names and any figure you would not want outside the company with placeholders you recognise, like vendor-A and price-A.

Paste the redacted chain and type: "List every decision actually agreed, every option still open, and every promise made by a named person with the date it was made. Quote the line it came from. Do not summarise what is not in the text."
Write the decision note under three headings: Decision, Cost, Owner and Date. Anything the model could not quote gets left out.
Open the thread again and check every claim in your four lines against the message it supposedly came from. If you cannot find it, delete it.
Reply on the same thread, subject line "DECISION — no further replies needed", and put the one person still owed a task in the To line.

flows.title: A handover you can still read at eight tomorrow morning
flows.job: Leaving a role, a shift or a project you ran alone
flows.who: the person leaving a job nobody documented while they held it
flows.situation: You are the only one who knows how the monthly report is built, which supplier always delivers late, and who to chase when the portal is down. You have two weeks, and you are not going to remember all of it on the last Friday.
flows.outcome: A handover doc with the recurring tasks, the systems and how to log in to each, the three things that always break, and where the files live.
flows.guard: Never write a password, a token or a client list into it — a handover doc gets forwarded, and you will not know to whom. Where only you know something, run the dictation on Your own laptop so nothing leaves the machine. The last step is you deleting whatever was never yours to write down.
flows.arrow: Google Calendar → Google Keep → ChatGPT → Google Docs → You → You
flows.prompt: Rewrite these as a handover for someone who has never done this job: one section per task with the trigger, the steps, the system it lives in, and who to ask. Then list the questions a total stranger would still have.

steps.do: Open the last month of your calendar and list every recurring meeting, deadline and report slot you actually have. That is the real job description.
Press the mic for each task and talk it through out loud as if you were standing beside the person: what triggers it, what you open, what you send, and what you do when it fails.

Paste the transcripts and type: "Rewrite these as a handover for someone who has never done this job: one section per task with the trigger, the steps, the system it lives in, and who to ask. Then list the questions a total stranger would still have."
Work through its list of missing questions and answer each one in plain sentences under the task it belongs to. This is the part only you can do.
Search the doc for passwords, client names, salaries and anything privileged, and strike every hit. Then delete anything you wrote that was opinion about a person.
Ask the person taking over to run one task with the doc while you stay silent. Every question they ask is a hole in the page, not in them.

flows.title: Tomorrow’s lesson for the half of the class that is lost
flows.job: A plan due tonight for a class in three levels
flows.who: teachers and tutors writing tomorrow’s plan after school
flows.situation: The topic needs nine weeks of prior knowledge and the class has four. Twelve are with you, eight are already behind, and three finished the work in the first ten minutes. The plan is due at 9 a.m. and you are out of evening.
flows.outcome: One lesson sheet with the same task at three entry points, the three questions you will ask, and a five-minute starter that tells you who is lost before you teach anything.
flows.guard: No pupil names, no SEN or IEP notes, no behaviour incidents and no class list in the chat box — describe groups by need only. What the model produces is a draft of your professional judgement, not a substitute for it: check it against your syllabus, your school’s safeguarding policy, and what you know these specific children cannot yet do.
flows.arrow: Phone notes → Claude → ChatGPT → Google Docs → You → You
flows.prompt: Write the same task at three levels: one for a pupil missing the prior step, one for the standard task, one stretch version. Same outcome, different entry. Give each a sentence I can read aloud.

steps.do: Write the single thing they must be able to do by the end of the lesson, plus the two most common ways this class fails it. Keep it in your own words.

Paste that plus the syllabus wording (no names) and type: "Write the same task at three levels: one for a pupil missing the prior step, one for the standard task, one stretch version. Same outcome, different entry. Give each a sentence I can read aloud."
Ask: "Design a five-minute no-writing starter that shows me instantly who cannot do the prior step. Tell me exactly what to look for in their answers."
Paste the starter at the top, the three versions side by side under it, and the timing down the margin in minutes, not idealism.
Read it against the room you actually have. Cross out anything that needs kit you lack, and every example that names a pupil or a family.
The next morning, read the sheet once before they arrive and run the starter yourself against the clock. Cut whatever spills past the bell.

flows.title: Forty copies of the same mistake into one fix and four exercises
flows.job: Marking the identical misconception all the way down the pile
flows.who: teachers and markers facing a full set of scripts tonight
flows.situation: Every paper has the same error — a sign dropped, a date attributed to the wrong person, the middle step skipped. You have written the same comment forty times and there are still twenty scripts in the pile.
flows.outcome: One shared feedback sheet: the misconception named plainly, why it happens, one worked example, and four practice items with answers underneath.
flows.guard: Never upload pupil work — a script has a name, a class and sometimes a diagnosis written on it. Type the misconception into the chat box, not the paper. The model cannot see the child: check that the examples use only notation you have actually taught, and that the practice answers are right yourself, because a model will build a wrong answer with total confidence.
flows.arrow: You → Gemini → Claude → Google Docs → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: Explain this misconception to a pupil who made it honestly: two sentences on why it feels right, two on why it is wrong, then one worked example that starts from where they went wrong.

steps.do: Write the misconception in one plain sentence, the exact line where it appears, and one real example of it with the numbers replaced by your own.
Type: "Explain this misconception to a pupil who made it honestly: two sentences on why it feels right, two on why it is wrong, then one worked example that starts from where they went wrong."

Paste the sheet so far and ask: "Write four practice items: the first a direct repeat, the second one small twist, the third a trap for this exact mistake, the fourth a transfer to a new context. Put the answers underneath, separated by a line."
Paste the explanation and the four items into one page headed with the misconception, answers on a second page so you can hand out only the first.
Work all four items closed-book and check the answers. Fix any that do not match, and delete any item needing a method you have not taught.
Write the single line that goes on every script pointing at the sheet, and add your own personal sentence for the handful whose error was a different one.

flows.title: A term notice into one page parents read on the bus
flows.job: The whole-term letter nobody opens
flows.who: teachers and year leads sending the same notices every half term
flows.situation: You sent a page of dates, kit, consent and policy. The reply is forty questions, nineteen of them answered in the first paragraph. Next term you get one screen, so it has to work on the first read.
flows.outcome: One page a parent understands in sixty seconds, plus the same content as a short plain message for whatever group channel the school already runs.
flows.guard: Never name a child, an incident, a family situation or a member of staff in a notice — and do not paste any pupil data into a chat box. A translated notice is still a legal and safeguarding document: your school’s policy owner or office manager signs it off before it leaves, and the dates get checked against the calendar, not the draft.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → ChatGPT → Gemini → Canva → You → Phone notes
flows.prompt: Rewrite this as one page for a busy parent: the three dates with what to do by each, what to buy or bring, what I must sign, and one line on who to contact. Delete everything that is not action, and mark anything you dropped as LEFT OUT.

steps.do: Open the notice you sent last term and copy it into a plain doc so the text can move cleanly.

Paste it and type: "Rewrite this as one page for a busy parent: the three dates with what to do by each, what to buy or bring, what I must sign, and one line on who to contact. Delete everything that is not action, and mark anything you dropped as LEFT OUT."
Paste the one page and ask: "Translate this into simple, natural [the language] at reading level A2, keep every date and number exactly as it is, and list any word you had to guess at."
Drop the text into a free one-page flyer template: dates first, one box per item, nothing smaller than 14 point, then export it as a PDF.
Read every date, amount, uniform item and contact against your own calendar and school policy. Open the translation and verify the digits did not move.
Hand it to one adult who has never read it and time them. Whatever they ask about is the line you still have to rewrite.

flows.title: A call log into the triage note a clinician can read in a minute
flows.job: A waiting list nobody can sort
flows.who: clinic admins, receptionists and care coordinators holding a queue
flows.situation: Forty people are waiting. Your notes are a call log, a paper form and three messages on your own phone. The clinician asks who is worst and you cannot answer fast enough to be useful.
flows.outcome: One de-identified spreadsheet, one row per patient: symptoms in their words, how long, risk flags copied from your clinic form, and a suggested order for the clinician to overwrite.
flows.guard: No name, no number, no address, no date of birth and no full record ever goes into a chat box — the model only ever sees the de-identified table, and anything too sensitive to leave the building gets done on Your own laptop. This does not triage anybody. It organises what a clinician triages: the ordering, the urgency and the referral decision stay with them, and a model must never be asked for a diagnosis.
flows.arrow: Your own laptop → Phone notes → Google Sheets → Claude → You → You
flows.prompt: Group these by the urgency criteria in my last two columns. For each row give one reason, and list every row where the information is too thin to judge. Do not diagnose anything.

steps.do: Open any spreadsheet on the machine and make one column per field: symptoms in the patient’s own words, how long, mobility, hearing, first appointment or review, and a red-flag column fed only by your clinic’s own written list.
Fill the table with what you actually have, using your initials or a reference number, never a name. Type the symptoms as they were said to you.
Copy in your clinic’s own red-flag criteria — the printed policy, not a model’s idea of one — so the flag column has a definition beside it.

Paste only the de-identified rows and type: "Group these by the urgency criteria in my last two columns. For each row give one reason, and list every row where the information is too thin to judge. Do not diagnose anything."
Check each grouping against the criteria and the flag column, then delete the model’s reason anywhere the source information was missing.
Give the sheet to the clinician as a draft to overwrite, say out loud which rows have thin information, and let them set the order. That handover is the whole point.

flows.title: Discharge instructions into the page the family can actually follow
flows.job: Instructions that are correct and never read
flows.who: nurses, clinic admins and discharge coordinators sending people home
flows.situation: You have handed over three pages of instructions. The next morning the relative telephones because nobody can tell which tablets stopped and who to ring at the weekend.
flows.outcome: One plain-language home page: what changed, what to take and what to stop, three things that mean call now, and one named contact for out of hours.
flows.guard: No patient identifier and nothing from the record leaves the clinic. Type the generic wording you are allowed to reuse, never an individual’s notes, and keep the medicine list out of the chat box. The clinician or pharmacist checks the dose, frequency and interactions against the discharge summary before anything is handed over — the family cannot check it, so someone qualified must. If there is no local plain-language or easy-read standard, get the communication lead to look at it before you print.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → You → ChatGPT → Gemini → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: Rewrite this as one page at twelve-year-old reading level. Keep every drug name, dose and number exactly as written. Add nothing that is not in my text. Put anything you were unsure about in a list at the bottom under NOT SURE.

steps.do: Copy your own clinic’s generic discharge wording into a doc. No patient name, number or record in the file.
Add, yourself, the four things that differ for this household: what changed, what stopped, what started, and the one thing that worries them most.

Paste the generic wording plus those four facts and type: "Rewrite this as one page at twelve-year-old reading level. Keep every drug name, dose and number exactly as written. Add nothing that is not in my text. Put anything you were unsure about in a list at the bottom under NOT SURE."
Paste the page back and ask: "Which of these sentences could a tired relative get wrong? Rewrite only those, and give me the three questions they will ask on the phone."
Read every drug name, dose, timing and warning against the discharge summary line by line. Delete anything sitting under NOT SURE until the clinician or pharmacist confirms it.
Print one copy for the patient and one for whoever is actually going to be at home with them, then read the three call-now items back to them before they leave.

flows.title: A thirty-page agreement into a list of what to push back on
flows.job: A contract you are not allowed to review
flows.who: paralegals and contract coordinators told to flag the issues by four o’clock
flows.situation: The counterparty sent a thirty-page agreement with six schedules, a redline from last year nobody kept, and a deadline this afternoon. You are not the lawyer, but you are the one expected to find what matters.
flows.outcome: A short issues list: each clause that changes what we do, its page number, what is missing or unusual, and a proposed position to put in front of the solicitor.
flows.guard: Confidential and privileged material does not go into any consumer chat box — a client contract, a matter file or anything under NDA stays on Your own laptop. The output is a triage list, not legal advice: a qualified solicitor signs off the position on every clause before it goes to anyone outside the firm, and a model will invent clause references that look precise, so each one gets opened.
flows.arrow: Your own laptop → Google Docs → Claude → ChatGPT → You → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: List every clause that changes what we must do, pay, deliver or indemnify. Give the page and clause number, what it says in one line, and what is missing compared to a standard position. Quote the wording you relied on.

steps.do: Save the agreement locally and confirm what you are allowed to process off it before any chat box opens.
Copy the agreement into a doc, drop the headers, the notices page and any schedule that is not ours, so the pasted text is only clauses.

For anything not confidential, paste the text and type: "List every clause that changes what we must do, pay, deliver or indemnify. Give the page and clause number, what it says in one line, and what is missing compared to a standard position. Quote the wording you relied on."
Paste the same text to a second model and ask the same question, then type: "Now list only the clauses the first pass might have missed."
Work through both lists and find each clause in the real document. Delete any reference you cannot locate and any line that is not actually quoted in the text.
One row per surviving clause: page, what it says, why it matters to us, and our proposed position with the alternative wording left blank for the solicitor.
Send the list to the qualified solicitor with the contract attached and mark anything touching liability, data or termination as needing their words, not yours.

flows.title: An access request you have to approve or refuse, with a written reason
flows.job: The request that needs a rationale, not a yes
flows.who: compliance officers and paralegals handling records, subject or disclosure requests
flows.situation: Somebody wants a folder, a dataset or a file. Policy says you decide, and says you give a reason in writing. You have approved two today already and you wrote one sentence each time, because that is what everyone does.
flows.outcome: A decision record per request: what was asked, the test you applied in your own words, the reason for the outcome, what is being withheld, and the named approver who signed it.
flows.guard: Never paste the requested material into a chat box — a model sees the request wording, nothing else, and the content stays on Your own laptop. This flow writes the reason; it does not make the decision. The legal or compliance owner who holds the delegation signs it, and anything touching privilege, a third party’s data, a safeguarding record or litigation gets escalated to them before a decision is drafted.
flows.arrow: Google Docs → Phone notes → Claude → You → Google Sheets → You
flows.prompt: Against this test only, list the questions I must answer before deciding, split into what the request clearly covers, what it clearly does not, and what I cannot tell from what I have described.

steps.do: Copy the one test you are actually meant to apply from your own written policy — the wording, not a paraphrase — into a blank doc.
Type what was requested, by whom, for what stated purpose, and which category of material it touches. No content, no names of third parties.

Paste the policy test plus your description and type: "Against this test only, list the questions I must answer before deciding, split into what the request clearly covers, what it clearly does not, and what I cannot tell from what I have described."
Work through its questions in your own words and mark every one you cannot answer from the file in front of you. Those are the ones you chase before you decide.
Add one row: date, requester, what was asked, test applied, outcome, the reason in a sentence, what is withheld, and the approver’s name.
Send the reason to the person holding the delegated authority for sign-off before the reply goes out, and keep their confirmation with the log row.

flows.title: The same ticket nine times this week into one reply and one real fix
flows.job: A queue full of one error
flows.who: service desk agents and IT support owners with a repeat offender in the queue
flows.situation: The same error, nine times, four different people. You have answered it nine times by hand. Nobody has written down what it has in common, and nobody owns the fix.
flows.outcome: A known-error entry: symptom, what it has in common, the workaround that actually held, a canned reply, plus one root-cause ask with the evidence attached.
flows.guard: Never paste logs, tickets or mailbox contents that hold usernames, IP addresses, hostnames or anything user-identifying — strip them first, or run the whole analysis on Your own laptop. A model will pick a confident cause from sparse data, so the cause you send to engineering is the one you reproduced yourself, and the fix ships only after someone with the access has tested it on a machine that is not the only one broken.
flows.arrow: Chrome → Google Docs → ChatGPT → Perplexity → Google Docs → You
flows.prompt: What do these nine have in common: same trigger, same version, same time of day? Then write the four-line workaround reply an agent can paste, and the one root-cause question engineering needs. List anything you are inferring rather than reading.

steps.do: Open each ticket and copy its subject, first message and resolution into one block of text, with nothing that identifies a user or a machine.
Replace every name, IP, hostname and mailbox with placeholder text you can map back locally if you need to.

Paste the redacted block and type: "What do these nine have in common: same trigger, same version, same time of day? Then write the four-line workaround reply an agent can paste, and the one root-cause question engineering needs. List anything you are inferring rather than reading."
Take only the exact error string, with your details removed, and search for it: "Show me the vendor pages that use this exact wording, with dates, and whether a patch exists."
Add one entry to your team’s doc: symptom, cause you have actually confirmed, workaround, ticket count, and the escalation with the evidence attached.
Reproduce the fault on one machine before you call it a cause, and check the workaround line reads like something you would send a human.

flows.title: The access request that is always one checkbox away
flows.job: Answering the same access question in person all day
flows.who: IT admins and helpdesk agents who keep walking someone through a form
flows.situation: Twice this week you have had a message that turns out to be one unticked box on a request form. Both people waited a day. Both could have fixed it in ninety seconds if the page had told them the box exists.
flows.outcome: A one-page access FAQ: the six requests people actually make, the exact field or checkbox for each, where to go, and the four lines that mean a human has to intervene.
flows.guard: Never put a real system name, account, group, role or URL you would not publish internally into a chat box — describe systems generically, and keep anything close to credentials out of the flow entirely. Check every path and field name against the live form yourself: a model will invent a tidy workflow that no screen contains, and an FAQ that sends people to a button that does not exist costs you more tickets than no FAQ at all.
flows.arrow: Gmail → Claude → Chrome → Google Docs → You → Google Docs
flows.prompt: Group these by whether the person could fix it themselves from a form. For each group say what information they would need before they start, and which ones genuinely require an admin to act.

steps.do: Search your own inbox and the shared mailbox for the access requests of the last month and copy the questions, not the answers, into one list.

Paste the list and type: "Group these by whether the person could fix it themselves from a form. For each group say what information they would need before they start, and which ones genuinely require an admin to act."
Open each request form and note the exact field, checkbox or drop-down that answers it, with the wording the screen actually uses.
Six questions, each with the one field that decides it and a link. End with the four cases where a human must step in and who to message.
Follow every route in the document on a live screen. Delete anything you cannot reach, and fix every word the form does not actually say.
Add the page link to your standard reply so the next request is one click, then tell whoever owns the request form that it exists.

flows.title: The mess of data pasted into your sheet turned into something readable
flows.job: A number question with no explanation attached
flows.who: analysts and the office IT person who becomes the spreadsheet
flows.situation: Somebody has pasted two thousand rows into your sheet, three dates in three formats, an ID column where the zero got eaten, and no idea what the columns mean. They want the answer by three.
flows.outcome: A cleaned table plus one paragraph in plain English that names what was fixed, what was dropped and what is still unknown.
flows.guard: Redact before you paste, not after — names, account numbers, email addresses and anything user-identifying go, and if the file is a data subject’s file it stays on Your own laptop. A model will silently invent column meanings and drop rows it finds awkward, so the plain-English note must list every change it made and you must reconcile the row count before you send the answer.
flows.arrow: Google Sheets → Google Sheets → Excel → Google Sheets → Gemini → You → Google Sheets
flows.prompt: Clean these into one table: one date format, one number format, leading zeros restored on the ID column. Split each problem into its own column and write a plain-English note on what you changed. Do not interpret or aggregate anything yet.

steps.do: Duplicate the data into a new sheet and work only on the copy, so the original stays untouched and provable.
Remove every column a stranger should not see, then add a column asking the owner what each remaining header actually means.

Paste the redacted rows into a blank web workbook and type: "Clean these into one table: one date format, one number format, leading zeros restored on the ID column. Split each problem into its own column and write a plain-English note on what you changed. Do not interpret or aggregate anything yet."
Paste the clean version beside the original and the change notes on a second tab.
Once the shape is clean, paste twenty sample rows and ask: "Given these columns, what are the three questions this data can actually answer, and what would it badly mislead someone about?"
Compare the row count of the copy against the original, and spot-check five random values. If the model dropped or merged anything, you will only catch it here.
Reply to the owner with the answer, the three fixes you made, the rows you dropped and the one column you still do not understand.
